rows: Repetition of a word/phrase at the start of successive clauses
"We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields..." (Churchill)
Builds intensity; creates rhythm; signals determination
Repetition at the END of successive clauses
"Government of the people, by the people, for the people." (Lincoln)
Creates emphasis through reinforcement; final word most stressed
"When you call it a tax, they say no. When you explain that it's a fee, they say no."
End of one clause = start of next
"Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate. Hate leads to suffering."
Clause begins and ends with the same word
"The king is dead, long live the king."
Creates circular closure; the word "frames" the content
Repetition of a word/phrase with a few words between
"Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers"
Euphony; memorability; playful or portentous depending on context
"The rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain"
"Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country." (JFK)
Creates perfect balance; memorable; the reversal forces reflection
"To err is human, to forgive divine." (Pope)
Same grammatical structure for parallel ideas
"I came, I saw, I conquered." (Caesar: veni, vidi, vici)
Speed, urgency, forward momentum; the list arrives fast
"And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew..." (Matthew 7)
Compact, rhythmic, equal weight; easy to remember
Omission of words understood from context
"Some have greatness thrust upon them." (not "some [people] have greatness thrust [upon them]")
Insertion of a qualifying thought mid-sentence
"The general (who had not slept in 36 hours) ordered the advance."
Adds information while maintaining main flow
"If you do that again, I will—"
Creates threat by omission; the imagination supplies the ending
Mentioning something by saying you won't mention it
"I won't even bring up your voting record."
Introduces the very thing denied; ironic emphasis
"Life is a journey." "The meeting was a minefield."
Creates new understanding by mapping one domain to another; cognitive efficiency
Explicit comparison: A is like B
"He fought like a lion." "My love is like a red, red rose."
Softer than metaphor; keeps the comparison visible
Replace a thing with an attribute/container
"The White House announced..." (= the President) "The pen is mightier than the sword." (= writing/power)
Economy; the substitution focuses attention on the relevant attribute
Part for whole (or whole for part)
"All hands on deck." (hands = sailors) "Nice wheels." (wheels = car)
Compression; the part selected is the relevant part
Proper name used as a common noun (or vice versa)
"He's a real Einstein." "The Napoleon of crime."
"The arm of the chair." "The head of the corporation."
Some are so established they're no longer felt as metaphors; conscious catachresis creates surprise
"I've told you a million times." "He's the greatest engineer in history."
Emphasis through excess; the exaggeration signals emotional intensity
Understatement, usually by negating the opposite
"Not bad." (= very good) "He's not the sharpest tool in the shed." (= he's dull)
Ironic understatement; leaves gap for the audience to fill; British understatement
Saying the opposite of what is meant
"Oh yes, that's a brilliant plan." (= terrible plan) "He was hardly a saint."
Forces the listener to decode; creates sophistication; can be cutting
Apparent contradiction in two adjacent terms
Creates tension; forces reflection; signals complexity
Attributing human qualities to non-human things
"The market fears inflation." "The code is lying to you."
Makes abstract forces graspable; evokes emotional response
Direct address to an absent or abstract entity
"Death, be not proud." (Donne) "O Liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!"
Elevates the addressee; creates dramatic presence; emotional intensity
Extended metaphor where a whole narrative means something else
Allows indirect communication of a message; creates protective distance
Question posed for effect, not answer
"Is the Pope Catholic?" "Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?"
Forces the audience to supply the obvious answer; creates engagement
Speaker asks a question and answers it
Controls the objection by raising and answering it preemptively
Imagining and responding to possible objections
"You might say... But I would answer..."
Repeat at start: "We will X, we will Y"
Building emphasis in speeches; lists with urgency
Repeat at end: "X of the people, Y of the people"
Add conjunctions: "X and Y and Z"
End = Start: "fear leads to anger. Anger leads to..."
Explaining the abstract through the concrete
Compression; the salient part made visible
Dramatic presence; elevation of a concept
Build intensity with repetition in a speech
Clarify a contrast between two options
Make a list feel urgent and fast
Make a list feel cumulative and weighty
Explain a complex technical concept vividly
Control an objection I know is coming
Add emotional weight to a ceremonial speech
